feedback: If the child counts wrong faces (e.g. four rectangles, or two triangles and two rectangles), hand them the target prism and match each of its faces to a net shape before deciding; count faces first.

For an arrangement failure, have the child trace which edges will meet when folded and find where faces overlap or leave a gap. Rearranging into a band of three rectangles between the two triangular ends is one reliable fix, though not the only valid net.
A sorting task like this can check and build classification of nets, but it does not itself elicit independent construction of a net from scratch; use it alongside, not instead of, building.
activities.intendedInsight: Nets fail for two distinct reasons — the wrong set of faces, or a correct set arranged so it cannot close — and the same solid can have more than one valid net.
learnerActions: Given several candidate nets for a triangular prism, sort them into those that will fold shut and those that will not.

For each failing net, say whether the problem is the face-set (wrong shapes, wrong number or mismatched sizes) or the arrangement (correct faces placed so that, when folded, some overlap or leave a gap).
Find two different valid nets for the same prism and explain why both work.
Reason about a near-miss: if a net has three triangles and two rectangles, could it fold into this prism, or into any closed solid at all? Explain using the faces a triangular prism needs.
activities.title: Compare and diagnose nets for the same solid
